newsitem.title: GHANA: British firm halts Ghana Airways losses.
newsitem.headline: British firm halts Ghana Airways losses.

text.p: State-owned Ghana Airways has shown its first profit since 1992 and appears on course for eventual privatisation, Chief Executive Rex Lezard said.
Lezard said in an interview unaudited accounts for calendar 1995 showed the airline made a pre-tax profit of 650 million cedis, against a loss of 1.2 billion cedis in 1994.
Lezard is from wholly owned British Airways unit, Speedwing Consulting Ltd, which won a two-year management contract in July 1995 to prepare the carrier for privatisation.
"The airline has suffered over the years, year after year of loss and we are forecasting a profit for 1995," Lezard told Reuters. "It is a very modest profit but it is a move in the right direction."
Lezard expects pre-tax earnings for full-year 1996 to be between 2.5 billion and three billion cedis if the company's reform programme cost-cutting remains on track.

Speedwing's contract ends next July, when the Ghana government expects it to have transformed the airline into a profit-making company. Then the government will decide on selling off the national carrier or part of it.
Except for 1992, Ghana Airways has lost money every year since 1988, according to its books, seen by Reuters.
In 1992, Speedwing took over management of Kenya Airways. Four years later, last May, Dutch KLM bought a 26 percent stake in the airline.
But Lezard cautions against comparisons between the two African carriers.
"Kenya Airways was a much bigger airline to start with, carrying far larger numbers of passengers and freight," he said.

"Our job is to get this airline (Ghana Airways) to a stage where the government can decide that they wish to divest. To reach that stage you have to operate as a limited liability company with a strong balance sheet and good profits and loss accounts," Lezard said.
In 1995 Ghana Airways carried 187,500 passengers against 182,278 the year before. Uplifted freight was almost 5,150 tonnes in 1995, against 4,988 tonnes in 1994.

Available seat-km (ASKS) were a little over one billion km in 1995, compared to 992 million km in 1994, while occupied seat-km (RPKS) were 601 million km in 1995 against 477 million km the year before.
The carrier's turnover in 1995 was 101.5 billion cedis, nearly double the 65.2 billion cedis in 1994.

Operating costs for its fleet of two planes at the time was 62.9 billion cedis for 1995, against 44. 8 billion cedis in 1994. General and admnistration costs in the same comparative periods were 37.8 billion cedis vs 21.5 billion cedis.
The Ghana Airways fleet consists of two fully owned aircraft -- a 15-year old DC-10 and an 18-year old DC-9.
As part of the rehabilitation plan, the company leased a 23-year old DC-10 from Belgian Skyjet in May this year.
The extra plane was badly needed to boost exploitation of existing routes, Lezard said, adding:

"We were fortunate to have a very strong network of routes. The routes to Europe, the United States and South Africa form a three-legged stool for serving West Africa as a regional hub. But we had to increase frequency and that meant expanding our fleet."
By the end of this year, Ghana Airways hopes to obtain a second DC-9 for its regional service.

"We want to improve the quality and increase the frequency of flights. Ghana Airways provides most of the travel along the west coast but sometimes it is a bit like a tro-tro (Ghanaian minibus), with too many stop-overs," said Lezard.
In June Ghana Airways increased its weekly flights to London from three to four, while once-weekly flights to New York and Johannesburg became twice-weekly.
